newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Tickle me durables.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Tickle me durables.

text.p: Now that the Tickle Me Elmo fever has subsided, U.S. credit market participants can begin to focus on something they normally thrive on: economic data.

Although the 0830 EST/1330 GMT release of durable goods orders for November is not likely to stir as much excitement as one of this year's hottest selling toys, experts said Friday's data may draw some attention.

"If you get a big move one way or another way in non-defense capital goods orders, particularly the non-aircraft, non-defense capital goods orders, you could see some market movement," said Elliott Platt, managing director of economic research with DLJ Securities Corp.
Platt noted that many market participants are off on holiday, so the response to the statistic may be muted or exaggerated.

Forecasting a 0.5 percent decline in the headline durables number, Platt said he is calling for a decline in aircraft orders, an increase in defense capital goods orders and flat non-defense, non-aircraft orders.
In a Reuters survey, the average forecast of 22 economists expect the Commerce Department's report on total orders rose 0.1 percent in November versus a 0.3 percent rise in October.
The forecasts, however, ranged widely from a low of down 1.5 percent to a high of up 1.8 percent.
Don Fine, chief market analyst with Chase Asset Management, said he is also predicting a modest change in orders, which should result in a tepid bond market reaction.
"I'm leaning a little more on the plus side than on the minus side," he said, explaining that numerous (Boeing) aircraft orders have not yet made their way into the November data.
"If the number is flat, give or take a little, I don't think there is going to be a major reaction," he added.
Indeed, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond yield should cling to its current trading range of about 6.50 to 6.75 percent Friday, experts said.
In addition to durable goods orders, weekly U.S. jobless claims data are slated for release at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.
Wall Street experts forecast, on average, claims fell to 346,000 in the week ending December 21, from 351,000 in the previous week.
Astrid Adolfson, first vice president and an economist at MCM Moneywatch Inc, said uneven holiday work closures push claims lower.
But the bond market is not expected to get jolted by a modest drop in jobless claims data, she said.
"We don't think the labor market is as weak as in the numbers we are suggesting now, we just think it is faulty seasonals," she said.
